extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners and attorneys subject to USPTO discipline (and counsel handling USPTO reciprocal-discipline matters)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements governing imposition of reciprocal discipline by the USPTO when a state disciplinary body has imposed public discipline on a practitioner. Covers the Selling v. Radford presumption, the limited grounds for avoiding identical federal discipline, notice requirements, and related procedural consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption in favor of imposing reciprocal discipline (Selling v. Radford)
rubrics_metrics.description: A state disciplinary action creates a federal-level presumption that imposition of reciprocal discipline is proper (Selling v. Radford, 243 U.S. 46 (1917)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO Director begins with the presumption that identical discipline is appropriate based on the state's adjudication; the practitioner bears the burden to overcome that presumption by clear and convincing evidence of one of the narrow Selling-based exceptions. Federal review is narrow and not a general rehearing of the state proceedings (courts are not sitting to discover error in the state court's proceedings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory/regulatory requirement to impose identical discipline unless narrow exceptions shown
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1), the USPTO Director shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates a genuine issue of material fact as to specified exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation mandates imposing the same form of public discipline that the state imposed unless the practitioner meets the strict exceptions detailed in the regulation. The types of discipline enumerated are to be mirrored federally (public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, disciplinary disqualification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner's burden: clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid imposition of identical reciprocal discipline, the practitioner must 'clearly and convincingly demonstrate' and raise a genuine issue of material fact as to one of the enumerated grounds in § 11.24(d)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The burden of proof is on the respondent; courts construing similar reciprocal-discipline rules have repeatedly held that the respondent must meet this heightened evidentiary standard (e.g., In re Kramer, In re Friedman). Mere disagreement or assertion is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process ground (lack of notice or opportunity to be heard)
rubrics_metrics.description: One permissible ground to avoid reciprocal discipline is that 'the procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent must demonstrate that the state procedure deprived them of notice or a meaningful opportunity to be heard. The USPTO's review is limited — it examines the record for objective due-process defects, not to reweigh evidence. Examples/case law indicate this is a narrow inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infirmity of proof ground (insufficient evidentiary basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Another ground is that there was such 'infirmity of proof establishing the conduct' as to give rise to clear conviction that the Office could not accept the state adjudication as final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practitioner must show significant evidentiary flaws in the state proceeding such that the Office cannot accept the finding. Case citations emphasize that demonstrating infirmity of proof requires clear and convincing evidence and is narrowly applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave injustice ground (punishment disproportionate to misconduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: A third ground is that imposition of the same discipline 'would result in a grave injustice.' The 'grave injustice' analysis focuses on whether the severity of the punishment 'fits' the misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevail the respondent must show by clear and convincing evidence that the state's punishment was so ill-fitted to the adjudicated misconduct that reciprocal discipline would be unjust. Precedent instructs inquiry into whether the penalty was within the appropriate range for the misconduct (examples: In re Thav; In re Kramer; Matter of Benjamin). Admissions by respondent and the nature of the offense weigh against finding grave injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nunc pro tunc/retroactive start-date preconditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Retroactive (nunc pro tunc) imposition of reciprocal discipline to the date the practitioner voluntarily ceased practice before the USPTO is possible only if the practitioner complied with the precondition of providing prompt notice of the state disciplinary action to the USPTO within 30 days (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary cessation of practice alone does not suffice to obtain a retroactive start date. The practitioner must have timely notified USPTO of the state discipline (within 30 days); failure to do so (e.g., a multi-year delay in notice) defeats nunc pro tunc relief. The page emphasizes that Respondent's four-year delay in notifying USPTO foreclosed retroactive credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to notify USPTO of state discipline within 30 days
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are required by regulation to provide prompt notice to the USPTO of any state disciplinary action (precondition referenced in 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely notice enables certain procedural outcomes (like possible retroactive imposition); failure to notify timely is a substantive regulatory noncompliance that may affect relief and is relevant to the Director's decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and scope of notice to be published and disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall make public a Notice in the Official Gazette and give notice pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.59 of the public discipline and reasons for the discipline to state disciplinary agencies, courts of admission, and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Notice will describe the facts leading to discipline (conviction, state findings, rules violated) and announce the USPTO action; disciplinary decisions are available via OED's FOIA Reading Room. This is part of the expected follow-up after imposition of reciprocal discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative consequences tied to USPTO practice accounts and PKI
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon suspension, the USPTO may dissociate the respondent's name from any Customer Numbers and the public key infrastructure (PKI) certificates associated with those Customer Numbers, and prohibit the practitioner from applying for or obtaining a USPTO Customer Number or having their name added to one until reinstatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are standard administrative consequences ordered in tandem with suspension to prevent the suspended practitioner from practicing before the Office or using USPTO electronic credentials until reinstated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of judicial review under 35 U.S.C. § 32
rubrics_metrics.description: Review of the USPTO Director's final decision may be had by filing a petition in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, in accordance with 35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. § 11.57(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners dissatisfied with the Director's final order have a statutory avenue for judicial review; timing and procedural requirements under § 32 and the cited regulation govern that review.
